entries.text: For Need for Speed cinematics, Deenen's team once sweetened engines with layered bears, pigs, tigers and leopards for emotion; by NFS Shift they had moved on to distortion and synth sweeteners riding on top of real car recordings.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: "Need For Speed" [Exclusive Interview]

entries.text: To capture car crashes for Need for Speed, the team put an SM57 right at the point of impact, inside the collision itself, rather than relying only on safe distant perspectives.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: "Need For Speed" [Exclusive Interview]

entries.text: For each project I always look for the single “it-factor”.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Exclusive Interview

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Exclusive Interview

entries.text: Deenen treated weekend film-trailer jobs, starting with Daredevil and running past sixty titles, as his training ground: brutal deadlines forced odd, inventive solutions he then carried back into his game sound work.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Exclusive Interview

entries.text: On NFS Shift he chased what a driver actually hears mid-race using deliberately atypical sounds; that driver's-eye bed ended up becoming the signature sonic identity of the game's FMVs and menus.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Exclusive Interview

source.title: Charles Deenen on Sound Design for Games

entries.text: I often start from the smallest: one-inch stereo Radio Shack speakers at very low volume.

source.title: Charles Deenen on Sound Design for Games

entries.text: To fatten a sound, Deenen stacks two Renaissance Bass instances tuned to different frequencies so both sub and low-mids grow; on L1, he shortens release for more grit and lengthens it for a smoother result.

source.title: Charles Deenen on Sound Design for Games

entries.text: Never edit exactly “on the cut”.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Move the sound out of the picture, don’t just stop it

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Trailer triage: on the first watch, note only what grabs you and sound just those moments. On later passes add what serves story, pace or music, then strip out anything that is merely noise.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: In trailers, Deenen retimes the edit to his sound's rhythm in Pro Tools and hands the picture editor an OMF or edit list to conform, because editors cut better when inspired by the pacing of sound and music.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: A practice drill he recommends: rebuild a favourite sound using only five random library sounds, one per category, for several days running. To reverse-engineer a reference, study each frequency band and play it at half or quarter speed.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Stuck for an idea? Deenen suggests humming or singing the sound you imagine into a mic and processing that, browsing a library at random, or simply laying sounds against picture until something sparks.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: To find the sweet spot on a car, sweep a small wind-protected lav around it in repeated identical moves while listening for more tone and less noise, and keep exhaust mics clear of the hottest, most turbulent air.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: His 100-whooshes method: fill 10–20 tracks with long continuous material, bus it to a few submixes loaded with Doppler, flangers and envelope filters, sidechain-duck the buses against each other, gate in hits at the peaks, then ride faders live and record take after take.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: 100 Whooshes in 2 Minutes

entries.text: Before booking a car-recording location, have someone rev a car about 50 feet away as a noise test, favour closed forest or private roads, find out how long the surface takes to dry after rain, and avoid quiet passes at peak bird and cricket hours.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Car Recording Guide

entries.text: For the Star Wars Battlefront trailers, Source Sound split Ben Burtt's original sounds into tonal and noise layers, kept the tonal core and rebuilt the noise in higher fidelity, giving them control in a dense mix.

source.title: The Sound of the Star Wars Battlefront Trailers

entries.text: We always tried to stay faithful, but enhanced it enough so that it punched more

source.title: The Sound of the Star Wars Battlefront Trailers

entries.text: Deenen's trailer mixes stay clean and punchy partly because every effect with hiss or noise runs through RX in real time; for mismatched dialogue he starts by using Ozone's Matching EQ to match one line to another.

source.title: iZotope Masters Q&A Series, Part 1

entries.text: His 'bigganizing' trick for explosions and guns: gain-clip a sound by around 20 dB, then run it through a de-crackler. The result feels huge and loud without audible distortion, which is all about perceived loudness.

source.title: Charles Deenen: Crafting Epic Sounds with Sonnox Plug-ins

entries.text: Need for Speed recorded every car with no turbo fitted so turbos could be layered back in as upgrades, and drove each one on real roads to capture authentic gear shifts with all their sputters and grunts.

entries.text: Minto captures gameplay footage and tracklays it like a film first, ignoring engine limits entirely; only once the ideal is clear does he work out how to make the game deliver it.

source.title: Ben Minto Unplugged

entries.text: Standing next to a real weapon or explosion, you feel how loud it truly is. Minto sees the designer's job as figuring out how to transmit that physical sensation, not just the recorded waveform, to the player.

source.title: Ben Minto Unplugged

source.title: Ben Minto on Game Sound Design

entries.text: To keep a gun feeling like it's in your own hands, Minto gives the weapon mechanism its own delicate, distinctive Foley layer, so the handling detail anchors the shot close to the player.

source.title: Ben Minto on Game Sound Design

source.title: Heard About: Battlefield 4

entries.text: On Battlefield 4, DICE took player Foley out of the HDR mix system so huge explosions could no longer cull your own footsteps, keeping a constant link between your character and the world.

source.title: Heard About: Battlefield 4

entries.text: Small personal details sell immersion: in Battlefield 4 a water sprinkler changes character when you stand beneath it, adding the sound of water striking your helmet.

source.title: Heard About: Battlefield 4

source.title: Heard About: Star Wars Battlefront

entries.text: Battlefront's sounds weren't bounced as final files; they were assembled at runtime from layers inside Frostbite, a workflow Minto likened to Max/MSP or Reaktor rather than a DAW, making them almost infinitely variable.

source.title: Game Audio: The sound of 'Star Wars: Battlefront'

entries.text: What you have to try and do is make the game sound like the film.

source.title: Ben Minto: Star Wars Battlefront sound design – 'We put a sound in with one in a million chance of it playing'

entries.text: To recreate blasters, Minto went to a guy-wire and struck it for that classic twang. He also slipped in Chewbacca's Tarzan yell with a one-in-a-million chance of ever playing.

source.title: Ben Minto: Star Wars Battlefront sound design – 'We put a sound in with one in a million chance of it playing'

entries.text: For Battlefront ambiences Minto recorded redwood forests for Endor, the far north of Sweden in midwinter for Hoth, desert for Tatooine and two weeks in Iceland, believing being there makes recreating the feel easier.

source.title: Ben Minto: Star Wars Battlefront sound design – 'We put a sound in with one in a million chance of it playing'

entries.text: Wind alone didn't make Hoth feel right, so the team layered in howling wapiti elk, a door creaking in a storm and the interior of a cave behind a frozen waterfall.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: Andersen first tried putting Limbo entirely in mono to evoke old film, but found it unengaging and not immersive; instead he distorted sounds and then re-widened them into an almost anti-phase spatial spread.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: Running everything in Limbo through an old tape machine glued the sounds into one family in the mix, and a spring reverb with its wet level at zero acted as a hardware filter, thinning sounds into something more generic.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: Limbo's soundscape is structured as a journey: it starts as fairly naturalistic forest and grows steadily more abstract, almost transcendent, as the game progresses.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: Andersen's rule for Limbo: the more recognisable a sound was, the more he distorted it. Voices or animals carried such strong associations they would wreck the atmosphere, so they stayed out.

source.title: The mad science behind Inside's soundtrack

entries.text: Inside's team put a wired contact mic into a professional sword swallower's stomach, recording internal body ambience and projecting sounds into it; a captured heartbeat became the metronome for the lineup puzzle.

source.title: The mad science behind Inside's soundtrack

entries.text: Following John Carpenter, Andersen leaves long stretches of Inside without music, then drops in distinct cues at chosen moments, and treats even footsteps as musical material.

source.title: The mad science behind Inside's soundtrack

entries.text: Andersen often imprints the spectral shape of traditional instruments onto non-instrumental sounds using convolution or match-EQ, letting the computer help orchestrate a soundscape.

source.title: Control & LIMBO composer Martin Stig Andersen finds beauty inside the darkness

entries.text: For Control's supernatural Hiss, he rubbed a friction mallet against the enclosure of an EMT plate reverb, grounding something otherworldly in a real physical source.

source.title: Control & LIMBO composer Martin Stig Andersen finds beauty inside the darkness

entries.text: Inside's environmental reverb came from sampling a flagship 1980s Roland R-880 hardware reverb and running it as convolution, and Andersen conveys space more through apparent source size than reverb.

source.title: Control & LIMBO composer Martin Stig Andersen finds beauty inside the darkness

source.title: Spectrum Analysis: Interview with Rob Bridgett

entries.text: Bridgett treats mix snapshots like camera lenses: a handheld-camera view, for example, can switch in its own chain of distortion, compression and high-pass filtering that exists only while that view is active.

source.title: Spectrum Analysis: Interview with Rob Bridgett

entries.text: A subtle gameplay cue: when the player ducks into cover, gently low-pass some of the gunfire, then lift the filter the moment they break cover.

source.title: Spectrum Analysis: Interview with Rob Bridgett

entries.text: Automatic priority and attenuation keep a busy game from becoming a cacophony, but you also need a manual override so a story-critical sound, like a single twig snapping, can beat the system.

source.title: Spectrum Analysis: Interview with Rob Bridgett

entries.text: When talking to narrative designers, Bridgett suggests not talking about sound at all: discuss what the character is feeling, then design audio that amplifies that emotion.

source.title: Spectrum Analysis: Interview with Rob Bridgett

entries.text: Try outdoor Foley: record footsteps outside during quiet hours with a variety of footwear, and back the mic off to capture natural reflections rather than a dead studio sound.

source.title: Spectrum Analysis: Interview with Rob Bridgett

entries.text: the loudest sound isn't necessarily always the most important.

source.title: The Future Of Game Audio – Is Interactive Mixing The Key?

entries.text: Layer snapshots hierarchically: a default snapshot sets base group levels, ducking snapshots multiply on top, and event overrides take over for scripted moments. Cap each bus's maximum attenuation so stacked ducks can't bury it.

source.title: The Future Of Game Audio – Is Interactive Mixing The Key?

entries.text: Snapshots needn't only move faders: Bridgett points out they can shift pitch, LFE send, 3D fall-off, speaker assignment or even listener position, and that the graceful transitions between them are the real mix.

source.title: The Future Of Game Audio – Is Interactive Mixing The Key?

entries.text: Ultimately, the mix of a game should be invisible to the consumer.

source.title: The Game Audio Mixing Revolution

entries.text: For Scarface, Bridgett and programmer Rob Sparks took the game to Skywalker Ranch and mixed it live on a control surface: around 150 snapshots, every cinematic with its own, plus global dialogue and interior-ambience ducks.

source.title: The Game Audio Mixing Revolution

source.title: Building an immersive soundscape in Shadow of the Tomb Raider – full Q&A

entries.text: In Shadow of the Tomb Raider, unseen creatures were placed off-screen in the middle distance rather than far away, because mid-distance makes players more uncomfortable; not knowing if a sound is real or imagined was the team's definition of fear.

source.title: Building an immersive soundscape in Shadow of the Tomb Raider – full Q&A

entries.text: The game's jungle ambience was authored as 3D objects by level editors and mixed in 7.1.4, essentially a VR approach to sound applied at vast scale to a non-VR game.
